title: Notes of Ministry - 22 - September 1974

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 22 - September (2398)/Notes of Ministry - 22 - Septem - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I desire to say a word of encouragement, dear brethren, about our committal to God’s testimony and His care of those that are committed to it. So much depends, I think, upon what comes first in our lives. You will remember that Jesus said, “Seek ye first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you”, Matthew 6: 33. One person said to Him, “Lord, suffer me first to go away and bury my father” (Matthew 8: 21), but Jesus says, “Seek ye first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you”, Matthew 6: 33.

Now the Lord would encourage us to do this practically, that it might not remain just a word of Scripture, but that first and foremost in our lives might be His interests. It is a challenge, but I think at the same time it is an encouragement, because we have the assurance that in all matters needed here the Father will care for us. Most of us show that we do not really believe that; our practice tests us. We speak of the Father’s care and then act as though it did not exist. But the Lord is not chiding, therefore I must be careful not to do that, otherwise I might be exposed myself. But what the Lord brings to us is for everybody, speaker and hearers alike, and I think He would raise the question with us as to what is first in our lives; what is first in our thinking; what is first in our practice, whether it is “the kingdom of God
and his righteousness” or our own position and prosperity in things which exist here which are but for a season.
I would have to admit that things here engage a lot of my time and attention. If I think of the twenty-four hours in the day I have to confess how little time I give to thinking of what Paul

said or thinking of things that are amiable, noble, and so on. My mind, as I excuse myself is, of course, necessarily engaged with matters here. Now the Lord would raise a question with you and me as to which comes first. If I have to acknowledge that my interests come first, let me acknowledge it and tell Him that the desire of my heart and soul is that His interests should be paramount in my life. Let each of us make a committal like that. Ruth made a committal like that. She had no outlook; she had no prosperous job; she was following a poor old widowed woman. That is what God’s testimony is outwardly. But she said, “Do not intreat we to leave thee, to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest I will go”, Ruth 1: 16. Think of a committal like that!

I would like to appeal to the younger men and younger women as to your committal to the Lord. You will find you will be very tested and exercised. Often you will find yourself deflected, maybe, and discouraged, but fundamentally I would encourage you to make what we might call a vow to put the Lord’s interests first, and He will see to yours. Most of us here will know what Mr. Taylor once told us, that he had found in his experience that the Father was more able to look after his interests than he was himself. I think each of us can prove that, and the Lord would have us to prove it in experience.

But then, added to that, we find the cares of the testimony. We have all been burdened at some time or another by them. Any person committed to the Lord will find the exercises connected with the maintenance of what is due to God. Now I think it is not to be a burden that should overcome us. I was interested the other day, and quite surprised, to see a remark of Mr. Darby which in effect was this. We are often so burdened with the cares of the assembly and matters relating to it that we overlook, or have little time for, the importance of the glad tidings. That rather pulled me up. Energy spent, care carried, burdens perhaps becoming depressing, tend to hinder the proclamation of the glad tidings and to check the spirit of evangelism which should be with every one of us. Because, after all, the testimony largely is the glad tidings, the expression of God towards men and His disposition toward them, His desire that they should be blessed.

Now when Paul says; “Be careful about nothing”, he means ‘nothing’. The Spirit of God uses the word “nothing”. So that we are not to be careful about our own matters, but I think also in confidence in God we should not be depressingly burdened by the cares of the testimony. We are not to be indifferent or careless, nor should we be lacking in exercise about them, but we should not be anxiously careful. Sometimes we act and speak as though everything depended on us, whereas the Father has put everything into the hands of Christ, the only perfect and competent Man, and the One who will carry everything through for God. My part is to relate myself to Him and to those who relate themselves to Him, and in quietness and confidence to go on. So Paul says, “Be careful about nothing”. Sometimes we limit that, I

think, to our own matters, our bread and butter, as we speak of it, and what we need so that we might be maintained in life here; but I think when he says “nothing” he means ‘nothing’, we are not to be anxiously careful about anything, “but in everything … let your requests be made known to God”. You think of opening out your heart to God; tell Him everything. You can tell God everything. What a wonderful God He is “but in everything, by prayer and

supplication … let your requests be made known to God”. That is very wonderful. I think of the word “supplication” entering into scripture. It is said elsewhere a centurion “came to him, beseeching him” (Matthew 8: 5); it is supplication, earnest entreaty. Well, the argument might be then, Is God reluctant to give? You never speak to God as though He were reluctant to give, or that something had to be forced from Him, speaking reverently, but He loves to see the earnest exercises and affection of His people expressed to Himself; so, “by prayer and supplication … let your requests be made known to God”.

Now the Lord would encourage us on this line, but I want to draw attention to this, that He does not say this to the Corinthians, he says it to the Philippians; that is, I think, to persons who were themselves committed. He speaks a little earlier of their fellowship with the gospel

“from the first day until now” (Philippians 1: 5); he is not thinking therefore simply of their circumstances but he is thinking of God’s testimony, and he says this to persons committed to it; so he says “Rejoice”. I could not say that I am a very good advertisement for that, often, not so; but he says, “Rejoice … again I will say, Rejoice”. These Philippians were sharing the burdens of the testimony with him; they were committed not
only to the testimony of the glad tidings but also to Paul who was a prisoner. What a wonderful privilege that is as well as a responsibility.
What I would desire for each of us, dear brethren, is that we might be more with God about His testimony, that we might firstly be committed to it so that we take up the word ‘first’;

“Seek ye first the kingdom of God”, and that then, as committed, we might approach God in this simple spirit of dependence and implicit confidence “with thanksgiving”. Do you find you often forget that? I do. I am so much occupied with what I need or even what the brethren may need that I fail to notice what they have received. You see so many needs among the brethren that you fail to see what the Lord has done. So he says, “with thanksgiving”. Beloved brethren, we have much for which to give thanks; we have brethren to walk with, lovers of the truth, those with whom we can sit down in simple happy conversation and listen to what the Lord would say to us. How much there is for which we can give thanks! This is not simply, I think, that we give thanks for all the material benefits that we have, which of course we have for a time, but we give thanks for the many blessings we have both temporal and spiritual, and give thanks above all for the beloved brethren; when Paul saw the brethren “he thanked God and took courage”, Acts 28: 15. There are some like that in these days, you know, so distant from their brethren that when they do get the opportunity to be among them they thank God and take courage. Let us be not only in the spirit of prayer and supplication but also of thanksgiving. There is an old hymn which says,
‘Count your many blessings, name them one by one, and it will surprise you what the Lord has done’. I think it will,

not only in temporal things but spiritual things. If you care to reflect on the positive movements of the Lord and what He has done, you will find many things for which to give thanks; and I think if we look around on the dear brethren here we can say, ‘Thank God’, and we can take courage and go forward.

Then he says, “and the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, shall guard your hearts and your thoughts by Christ Jesus”. Oh, beloved brethren, what a resource we have in God; here it is “the peace of God”. Is your heart, are your thoughts, garrisoned by the peace of God? You know there is an environment which is marked by peace; wonderful! There is no conflict there. Jesus is there having overcome, He has gone into it, and there is the peace of God which presides in that environment. I think it is known in the assembly, known amongst the saints, and I think as we approach God, and frankly, simply, open our hearts to Him, we shall find that His peace will guard our hearts and thoughts. I know there are many things to cause the brethren anxiety, many sufferings, we think of the loss of loved ones and the like, that while that is carried in the spirit I think at the same time the peace of God is to guard the heart and the thoughts so that the saints should not be overcome, they should not be depressed, feeling that all is lost. How could all be lost, dear brethren, when all is in the hands of Christ? Everything will be secured, our true David will recover everything, there is no doubt about that, then He will hold it all for God.
Then Paul goes on to speak about thinking, What do you think about? You see, to some extent you can govern what you think about. He says, “whatsoever things are true … think

on these things”. Now I think you would have to confess that you could go home and you could sit down and think about these things. You say, ‘Well, I have the dinner to cook’. Of course, but you can still think. There is time for thinking and deliberately giving ourselves to it. “Think of what I say”, 2 Timothy 2: 7. Many things come in, Satan catches away the word, thorns spring up, as we have been saying, but I believe the Lord would help us to be deliberate. It may not be very long, you young men and young women, but if you give time to think about the things that Paul said and to take account of what was seen in him you will be surprised at what the Lord will do for you.

When I was a young man we used to be encouraged to go home to the Lord and go over with Him what we had had in the meeting. Have you ever done that? You will find it is very profitable. Go over it with Him, tell Him the scriptures we read, tell Him the impressions you received, and as you go over it so it becomes enlarged, and at the same time you are giving the Spirit room to form you according to the word you have heard. You try it and see! Taste and see that the Lord is good, Psalm 34: 8. You will find as you are committed to what He is saying in a living way to the assembly you will be formed according to it and become useful to Him in His testimony, and all the time guarded by the peace of God.

Then a little later Paul says, having referred to himself, “and the God of peace shall be with you”. It is not now the peace of God but the God Himself of peace shall be with you. I believe God intends that we should experience this, come what may, dear brethren. How much comes in in the assaults

of Satan against the testimony of God, and I believe, as Mr. Darby said, our simple duty is to do what is right and go on in peace. Do what is right. You will be criticised—sure to be! You will always be able to look back and say, ‘Well, if I had my life over again’! You have heard that, I expect. ‘At this point I would have done that, and I certainly would not have had that

job, I would have taken another job because I have never liked the job I am in, and if I had my time over again I would not have lived in this locality, I would have lived in that locality’; many things we say like that. But that is not to be, dear brethren, and I think the Lord would help us to understand that, despite all our mistakes, where there is simplicity and humility and dependence and confidence in Him. He will strengthen us to go on in His testimony. So here it is, “the God of peace shall be with you”. He is the God of hope, but He is also the God of peace. May the Lord encourage us in this.
Now I want to speak about Jesus, because whenever we speak about Him we see a Person or have a Person before us who is just unique or just Himself. As we have said before, the word

‘unique’ does not really convey what is in mind because the word ‘unique’ can be applied to other people. Paul was unique in a certain way, but Jesus was just Himself. “Let not your heart be troubled; ye believe on God, believe also on me”, He says. Sometimes we have thought of this as being a comfort for persons in sorrow, and it has been used that way no doubt, bereavement and the like; but think of the circumstances in which Jesus was. Judas had just gone out and was about to betray Him; Peter was about to deny Him, and the rest to forsake Him and flee. Think of the circumstances in which Jesus was and yet He says, “Let not your heart be troubled”. The circumstances are not like those that we enjoy, they had no Government protection, no policeman to protect them if there should be any trouble or difficulty. They were themselves likely at any time to be destroyed in the same way that persons were seeking to destroy Jesus, and yet in those circumstances He says,

“Let not your heart be troubled; ye believe on God, believe also on me”. I think He is referring to believing on Himself as above, “ye believe on God, believe also on me. In my Father’s house there are many abodes”, they will never be removed or defiled, “I go to prepare you a place; and if I go and shall prepare you a place, I am coming again”.
I have asked the Spirit recently to revive in my soul the brightness of the coming of Jesus.

What about you? We go on in life and as we get older Satan even uses words of scripture to discourage such as “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick”, Proverbs 13: 12. When we are young we may be bright; we are converted, and think of the coming of the Lord, then perhaps having been on the road for forty years, fifty years, maybe more than that, and still the Lord has not come, and it is natural that gradually the brightness of it recedes. Is it so with you? It has been so with me. But I ask the Spirit to quicken my affections for Jesus and understand that simple word of Mr. Raven that the hope of the church is not really the coming of the Lord but the Lord Himself. It is not simply an event. It will, of course, be an event, but the hope does not subsist in an event but in a Person.

He Himself is the hope, and I think that is why He has given us the Supper, so that if we are left here He will come to us tomorrow morning and those that love Him will have the consciousness of His presence, and when He comes in you find the affections of the brethren are astir because He is present. We look forward to His actual bodily coming, but in the meantime week by week He has given us the Supper so that our affections might be kept fresh until the time when He actually comes to

take us out of this world altogether. What a hope, dear brethren! Not like men; they wonder what is going to happen. You find that if you speak to them; What will happen? Everything is becoming so sophisticated, and there is corruption in high places.

I have had an impression recently that one of the projects that the Lord will undertake when He comes is to simplify everything. Man has got himself into a right tangle with his computers and various machines, but is only showing his ineptitude and inability to handle anything; he has made it all so complicated; but when Jesus comes He will make everything simple. As Mr. Taylor says, man is not intended to have all these machines and go all over the place, but God has put in the earth and in the surroundings in which man is, everything that is needed to satisfy him. So that to find satisfaction you do not really need to go to America or anywhere else because your satisfaction is in the Lord; you only go there to see the brethren, not to see the sights, although you can see them incidentally, especially when you are young, but you go to see the brethren, those precious to Christ, and connected with His testimony. But when the Lord comes, of course, we shall be with Him and all the saints, every one of them and none omitted.

Then the Lord says, still in these circumstances, “I give my peace to you”. Think of His uninterrupted communion, dear brethren, the peace that was His. I have often thought of the Lord when He was in the boat and He lay on the pillow asleep; in such circumstances I would say a perfect Man perfectly relaxed in the implicit confidence that He had in His Father; and yet I find it difficult to relax in the relatively happy circumstances in which I am.

But you think of the Lord Jesus, “I give my peace to you—not as the world gives do I give to you”. This is giving, as the hymn says, ‘Not as the world, but shares all it possesses with its loved co-heirs’.

Then what I wanted to call attention to, is this reference to His Father. “Ye have heard that I have said unto you, I go away and I am coming to you. If ye loved me ye would rejoice that I go to the Father, for my Father is greater than I”. Now throughout this gospel in particular you will find that the Lord’s whole life, His motive and His object, was His Father, not Himself. No matter what circumstances He was in, it was His Father’s will; and as Mr. Darby so touchingly says, If His Father’s will required Him to do nothing, He did nothing except to lay His head on the pillow and go to sleep. You think of that! It is difficult for our minds, being what they are, to grasp the thought of a perfect Man, but that is what Jesus was; and here He says, “my Father is greater than I”. He always had His Father before Him, and He says, “ye would rejoice”; so, dear brethren, we are to rejoice. He has gone away to His Father, but He says this in the context of, “I have said unto you, I go away and I am coming to you”, not for you, but to you; that is, as we think of Jesus coming to us on the morrow, we rejoice because He has gone away to His Father. You see the point; I think in speaking of coming to us
He would have in mind that we should go with Him to the Father; that is what is before Him.

Now in chapter 17, He says, “I have glorified thee on the earth”, but He says, “Father, glorify thy Son”, but then He says, “that thy Son may glorify thee”. That was His object, that was His desire, that in His being glorified He might glorify the Father, and so from the position in which He now is He is glorifying the Father. Again Paul says in Philippians that Jesus has been exalted and every knee is to bow and every tongue is to confess that Jesus Christ is Lord—Why? “To God the Father’s glory”, Philippians 2: 11. All the time you will find the Lord Jesus had God His Father before Him. I wonder if we are like that. He would encourage us by His Holy Spirit to be with Him in what He has before Him in glorifying His Father. I think He is doing it now, and I do not doubt He is doing it among the saints, “I am glorified in them”, and as He is glorified “in them” the Father is glorified. How wonderful this is, dear brethren!

May the Lord help us so that we might not be unduly burdened by the care of things here, nor unduly burdened even by the cares of the testimony, but guarded by the peace of God and conscious of the presence of the God of peace and of the assurance of the Lord’s own words, that He is coming for us so that we might go to our prepared abode. May the Lord encourage every one of us and may we receive some permanent profit from these occasions today, as from all our occasions, for God the Father’s glory.

I have read from this section because it deals with two boys who were growing up, two boys born into the same family. They had the same father, they had the same mother, and they were twins. Esau was the elder, and it says that the boys grew. The parents would see their growth—they grew physically, but what I would like to speak of tonight is as to whether there is any growth proceeding in love for Christ. It is evident, as the record shows, that one of these boys despised what was really his, the birthright. The New Testament shows us that he became profane. It is very sad in a family when the elder one, who should give a right influence to those coming after, seeks to go off into the world.
I want to speak specially to you dear young people here tonight, because you are growing.

There are a good number of boys in this room and you have been born under the influence of godly parents, fathers and mothers who love Christ and love the glad tidings, love the things of God, and love the people of God. You have been born into that atmosphere and environment. You are accustomed to hear the Scriptures being read; you are accustomed to be in the presence of prayer when your father kneels down and prays; you are accustomed to your food being given thanks for every time you sit round the table. All that is bringing God into your life, the One with whom you, yourself, must have to do. Every one of you here must
have to do with God. And God is being brought into your life through the environment into which you have

been privileged to be born. That is a wonderful favour. Thank God if you have come under the influence of godly parents who love Christ and the things of Christ. They are wanting to bring you up, not for man’s world, which is soon to come down anyway, but for God’s world.
What a fine thing that is that there should be those concerned about you as to how you are going to grow in relation to being available for God’s world.

What you find in this poor world around us is that man is his own object, and this is man’s day; it is a little day, and all that man has built up in the great cities of the world is soon to come down. But God is carrying through His thoughts in smallness. He is carrying them through despite all that the enemy is doing in seeking to ensnare youth by what the world offers. Moses was a remarkable young man. He was brought up as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, and Pharaoh was the king of Egypt. He was brought up as a prince in the court of Pharaoh. There came a time when Moses made a decision. Then he esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than all the treasures of Egypt. I am specially speaking to you young boys here in this meeting tonight because there are many of you, and that is not by chance, and the fact is that you are growing, and God is drawing near to you that you might give Christ a place in your heart.

In this scripture it says, “The boys grew, and Esau became a man skilled in hunting, a man of the field”; that is, his outlook was toward this poor world with all its sport and entertainment, calculated to allure men and women and boys and girls. Then it says that Jacob was “a homely man, dwelling in tents.” That is, he was a simple man, dwelling in tents. The tent is a provisional thought. A tent is pitched for the night and taken down, and then pitched for another night. It involves this provisional time in wilderness life, and the wilderness journey. That is, we are not sending down our roots in this world that has given Christ a cross. In whatever way we have to touch this world we touch it as of necessity. We give God thanks for everything He gives us in His goodness, and find all that can be available in view, of His interests here. So Jacob was a homely man dwelling in tents.

Isaac loved Esau because venison was to his taste, and Rebecca loved Jacob. That is, Rebecca loved what God loved. God does not say that until you come to the last book of the Old Testament, when He says, “I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau”, Malachi 1: 3. God waits until the responsible history is finished until He says that. God, then, is giving you an opportunity.

We are all under trial and test from this viewpoint. There was a remarkable young man who was given a very distinguished place in Israel’s history; that was Saul, a man who naturally was attractive, head and shoulders above other men. God put him under trial and test. You get circumstance after circumstance when God is putting everything in his way favourably to see how he will answer to the test. Alas, Saul made shipwreck, and you find him dead, slain among the enemies of God’s people on mount Gilboa.

The time comes when you have to make a decision. You may be at the point of decision for Christ, and God is appealing to you tonight. He would ask you whether you have given your heart to the Saviour. You cannot be too young to do that. Samuel was a young boy when he gave his heart to God, when he listened to God speaking to him and answered, “Speak, Jehovah, for thy servant heareth”, 1
Samuel 3: 9. So maybe God is drawing right alongside you tonight and saying, “Samuel, Samuel”; He is, maybe, bringing you to the point of publicly confessing the name of Jesus.

Maybe, if I were to ask you personally you would tell me that you love the Lord Jesus. Is He not worth loving? You may tell me that you love Him, but have you reached the point in your history when you are prepared to confess His Name, to tell people that He is your Saviour, that He is your Lord?

It is a vital matter that you should establish, as early in life as possible, contact with the precious Saviour of sinners, who died on the cross at Calvary, shed His blood, and suffered in the sinner’s stead, the Lamb of God, the taker-away of the sin of the world. Very soon the Lord is going to remove from this world the effects of sin. He has put away sin by being made the thing itself, for He was made sin. He has taken it away sacrificially and has removed sin from before the eye of God. And very soon He is going to remove the effects of sin from this poor world.

So, as I said, these two boys come under the same instruction. It is a very sad thing when you find that, in a family, you get the same care, the same affection, the same teaching, the same influence, and some may decide to give up the birthright, that is, they seek to go into the world that has given Christ a cross. Sometimes you wonder why it is. Maybe it is to bring out divine feelings. God, through Isaiah, says, “I have nourished and brought up children; and they have rebelled against me”, Isaiah 1: 2. Those are the feelings of a father. It would bring out depth of feeling in persons who think for God, who feel like God, as to what God feels. How He felt Israel’s going away; how He feels about you if you are seeking this way, if your outlook is in relation to the world that gave my Saviour a cross.

So Jacob wants the blessing. I think that is wonderful! Is your heart such tonight that you are concerned that you get it, that you are determined to get the blessing? Peter at Jesus’ knees said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord”, and yet at Jesus’ knees he is going to get the blessing.

It is then, the history shows, that God deals with Jacob. He deals with him personally. Esau goes on his way and becomes an opposer. He becomes a profane person. Alas, there are many like that. But let it be that in your case you are answering to the opportunity that has been put within your reach in that you are opening your heart’s door and giving room to the Saviour.
Maybe, as I speak, the Lord is speaking to some of you young boys here. You are growing, and as you are growing physically it may be that the work of God is growing too, and

developing, and you are opening your heart and giving more place to Christ. And maybe tomorrow as you go out to school you will tell your companions that Jesus is your Saviour, and is your Lord, and as you confess His name you will find that that is a tower of strength.

That is present salvation. Not only are you then assured of salvation for eternity, a place with Christ in heavenly glory for all eternity, but you will know the blessedness of present salvation in a world of evil, where sin is so rife and rampant, a world out of which Christ has gone judicially.

The Lord Jesus in John’s gospel left this world judicially; He went out of it, as that gospel shows, having a judgment of everything that was in it. Therefore this world is already judged. Soon the execution will take place, and how terrible it will be for the persons who have not given their hearts to the Saviour. But you, who have had such advantage, I say to you, do not break down the hedge that, in divine care, God has placed around you through the influence of parental affection and the teaching of the Scriptures in your home. God has put you in that environment so that you might be blessed, so that you might early come to the Saviour for yourself, that you might not break down the hedge, because if you break down the hedge the serpent will bite, Ecclesiastes 10: 8. Oh, do not pull away the shoulder as they did when the prophet spoke, Zechariah 7: 11(A.V). It says they pulled away the shoulder, like a deliberate turning away from the influence of divine grace through God’s messengers.
Let it be that the word is coming into your heart and you are making resolves, it may be for the first time, that you are going to live your life for Jesus. You learn that little song—

I want to live for Jesus every day,
I want to live for Jesus come what may,
Take the world with all its pleasure,
I’ve a more enduring treasure,
I want to live for Jesus every day.
You young people, learn that, learn to sing it every day, and as you grow you will find that you are growing, too, and making room for Jesus in your heart.
I leave this appeal, because you are growing up; the time is so short; and if we remain here you will soon be up into your teenage years when you will be tested by what

this world has to offer. Let it be that in early days you learn to put your trust in the Saviour by faith. That is not only listening to your parents as they pray, but learning to speak to Jesus for yourself, and learning to speak to Him as knowing Him; not only to speak about Him, but to speak to Him as knowing Him.

We find these two histories go on. The one turns to the world; he becomes a profane person, Esau, the Edomite, the one who becomes violent; he pursued his brother with the sword, he cast off all pity; that is Edom, that is Esau. Jacob, on the other hand, comes through the

discipline of that life in his experience with God. He goes out a worshipper. What a wondrous triumph! As an old man who has come through years of discipline in the school of God and developed in the knowledge of God, he goes out a worshipper leaning on the top of his staff.

May the Lord grant that some impression may be left in some of the young minds in this company that the time is now, when you are growing, that you should grow in making more room for the Saviour in your heart, and find the enjoyment, the happiness, the peace, the confiding restfulness, that a link with Jesus would bring into your soul.

Our scripture says, “Confide in Jehovah with all thy heart, and lean not unto thine own intelligence; in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he will make plain thy paths”. It is like getting back to the centre—“In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he will make plain thy paths”. You are taking your bearings, as it were, in God’s presence. You want to find out where you are. How constantly we are faced with this, and we find out where we are as we get on to our knees. If I might speak as believer to believer for a moment, we find out where we are as we simply get on our knees and tell God just what our problems are; just spread them out before Him. These are inspired words, of course. In a certain sense some of what is written may have been beyond the writers, but generally they had some experience of what they wrote. The Scriptures were indited by the Spirit, so they have the authority of a divine Person. Although persons were used to write them, the Scriptures carry, not the authority of persons, but the authority of the Spirit of God. So we should pay attention to the Scriptures.

“Confide in Jehovah with all thy heart, and lean not unto thine own intelligence; in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he will make plain thy paths”. Now I think that most of us at some time have done this. Some problem, some question, it may be about a job; it may be about a new school, or a new class—you do not know what the teacher will be like; you do not know what the others will be like—and we are told to “confide in Jehovah with all thy heart”. Just tell Him about it. Learn to develop simple links in this sense with God Himself. You say, ‘I like to pray to Jesus’. Well, that is good. When we are young, especially, we like to speak to Jesus. He is the Saviour; He is a Man, now a Man in heaven, but He has been here, and He knows what problems are. I do not think you ever get beyond speaking to Jesus in this sense. And so if I say, ‘Speak to God’, I could just as well say, ‘Speak to Jesus’. You see, in this time when this person wrote, Jesus had not yet been born,

but the truth remains; it is just as valid all the same, so we could say, ‘Confide in the Lord Jesus with all your heart’. Tell Him about it. Of course it is equally true that you can speak to the Father. The Lord Jesus often encouraged the disciples to confide in the Father. On several occasions He spoke about Him—of how the Father cares for us, how He has affection for us, and that it was He who drew us to Jesus. In that beautiful section at the end of John’s gospel, the Lord said a great deal about the Father. All this is to encourage us to confide in the Father also.

I remember that when we were children we had little strips of paper about the size of dominoes, and they had just a word on them. On Sunday afternoon, when it was wet, we had to stop at home because it was a mile to the meeting room, and we used to stretch these strips out, to make up texts from a list. This was one of them, “Confide in Jehovah with all thy heart” (It was years afterwards, I suppose I was in my teens, before I really did). I can remember that text now on the floor. We only used to go into that room on Sundays, and we would kneel down there and stretch all these words out, “Confide in Jehovah with all thy heart”. One day, when I was facing a crisis, I remember learning to do that. They are very fine, you know, these experiences, and they remain with you; they are intended to remain with us, and to deepen with us, until it becomes, one might say, second nature to a believer always to refer everything to the Lord Himself.

Here is a problem; here is a question; here is a condition to be met. Shall I work it out? Shall I try to plumb the thing entirely by myself? We are expressly warned not to do that—“Lean not unto thine own intelligence; in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he will make plain thy paths”.

So the scripture goes on to speak about instruction, and even of His chastisement. God would use certain circumstances, trials, and experiences in our lives that we would rather not go through. God does that, you know. It is never envisaged that the pathway of the believer will be without its difficulties, but it says, ‘Do not despise it’. The writer to the Hebrews uses this scripture, “Despise not the instruction of Jehovah, neither be weary of his chastisement”. You might get, as we say, to the end of your tether, and often we make things worse for ourselves by rebelling against the situation in which we are. The Lord would appeal to us—in this scripture it says, “My son”—how affectionate—“Despise not the instruction of Jehovah, neither be weary of his chastisement; for whom Jehovah loveth he chasteneth”.

You might think that because you are chastened, because there is discipline upon you, because things are not easy, the Lord has ceased to love you; but this rather puts it the other way, that the very fact of your going through it is an evidence that the Lord loves you. It says,
“even as a father the son
in whom he delighteth”.
Paul adds something more to this. He says, “to the partaking of his holiness”, Hebrews 12: 10. It is a very deep matter, that we might be formed in that attribute which belongs to God, His holiness.

Well, I just leave these words with us, and I commend them to us all that we may learn what it is always to get before the Lord, firstly as to our sins, and then as to every subsequent matter. May it be so for His name’s sake.
